image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   A **grid of radar/spider charts** (one small radar chart per state).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples**: each state is shown in its own mini radar chart.  
   - No stacking.  
   - States are arranged in a **geographic-style grid layout** approximating U.S. state positions.  
   - Color is used to show an additional variable across the small multiples.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Small-multiple panel; text label inside each radar chart |
| Barrier category (Historic undervaccination, Socioeconomic barriers, Low health care resources, Poor health care access, Irregular medical care) | Categorical/nominal | Angular position / axis around each radar chart; axis labels shown in the example chart |
| Level/value for each barrier category | Quantitative | Radial distance from center; connected polygon shape/area in each radar chart |
| Overall level of concern | Ordinal or quantitative | Color/hue of the radar polygon/outline (green/teal = lower, purple/pink = higher, per legend) |

comments.raw_comment:
Notice:
Looking at the graph, I notice that the southern states seem to have some of the "largest" fingerprints out of all the states, and also pertain to a higher overall level of concern in vaccination status. The smaller fingerprints tend to belong more to the northern states, along with the overall lower level of concern. Going more in depth, the green states(low concern) have a relatively small fingerprint, but a few of the states have spikes in specific variables. The pink states(high concern) have a more circular and well-rounded shape, with equal data in almost every variable for most of its states.

Wonder:
The map shows us a distinctly split status of the states- northern states having less concern in vaccination, while southern states are struggling with a much higher concern. I wonder if this has to do with economic statuses, or bigger populations all in all. Are there too many people to have proper healthcare, or is it a matter of social behavior?

Impact to community:
From the data, Virginia is shown to have a typically less-concerning vaccination barrier issue, but has a big spike for the variable "Low Health Care". Other than this, Virginia seems to be on a good path to vaccination, with less overall barriers in the process. In a nation-wide mindset, southern states are struggling to get vaccinated- it will be harder in the big picture to go back to "normal", and to maintain a decreasing case count.

 "Vaccination Barriers- A Roadblock to Normality".

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that the southern states tend to have higher levels of concern for the spread of the Coronavirus. than the northern states due to the sufficiency of vaccination barriers. I also noticed that some states have more vaccination barriers than all other states including Nevada, Mississippi, Georgia, and Oklahoma. The high amounts of vaccination barriers could be due to the lack of architecture in the southern states. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder if other factors such as skepticism, amount of education, ethnicity, religion, etc. also contribute to the amount of vaccination barriers and if so, by how much. I also wonder why Indiana has such a high level of concern despite being in the northern part of the United States. 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
This graph impacts me and my community because although we want to reduce the amount of COVID-19 cases by getting everyone vaccinated, some states are limited by their own community.  This makes me want to help other states with getting access to the vaccine and encourage them to keep others safe.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice and wonder? 
The first thing I noticed was the stark contrast between the levels of concern in rural states and urban states. In rural states such as Texas and Arkansas, there are high levels of concern for many vaccination barriers such as irregular medical, poor health care access, and low health care resources. This is possibly due to a less dense population in certain regions, making it more difficult for residents to find clinics that offer abundant vaccines in a safe manner. On the other hand, urban states have minimal concerns regarding the vaccination barriers except for low health care resources. Seeing the spike in concern over that issue, I wondered if this was due to a denser population that required more health care resources at a faster rate. 

What impact does this have on you or your community?
According to the graph, New York's biggest concern on barriers is the socioeconomic barrier. In the region of New York where I live, this isn't as big of an issue as other places in New York such as New York City and lower-income neighborhoods. However, people in my community still may have trouble accessing the vaccine due to these socioeconomic barriers. 

What's going on in the graph? Write a catchy headline.
Urban vs. Rural States in Handling the Vaccine

comments.raw_comment: I have noticed that the Northern states have major coronavirus vaccination barriers than the Southern states. That means that the Southern states have lower vaccination barriers than the Northern States. I wonder if these issues have to do with the lack of resources that the Northern States are facing. Also if it has more to do with the political demographics of the population or the population as a whole. The impact that this graph has on me and my community are it keeps us informed about the situation that is happening in other nearby states. In addition, it gives me an idea of how well my own state is doing in terms of COVID vaccination and the barriers. I have come to find that the state of Massachusetts has fewer cases of COVID and we are in a low range of coronavirus vaccination barriers. I understand that other states may not be so lucky because they have lower health care, poor health care access, irregular medical care, and historic under vaccination. The fifty-state graph is showing me the vaccination roadblock when it comes to taking the vaccination shoot. If I could rename this graph I would call it the "Struggle to  Receive Vaccination Shots in the United States."

comments.raw_comment: I notice that this is a graph informing us of the barriers to rapid vaccination by state in the United States. I can see that many states in the south are purple, meaning they are high risk, and tend to have the most barriers to the Covid-19 vaccine. Many of those states suffer from socioeconomic barriers, low health care, poor health access, and irregular medical care. I can also see that many states in the north also struggle with socioeconomic barriers primarily, but they are marked blue for low risk areas. I wonder as to why it is that we see much more concern and lack of medical care in the south than we do in the north. My first guess would be that the Northeast specifically has always excelled in medical advancements and medical care -- so it makes sense that they are doing well distributing coronavirus vaccines. My second guess is that the southern states tend to be very Republican leaning, and many people who are Republican are hesitant towards getting the vaccine. It could very much be that they are unsure and a little nervous to get it. It could also just be the socioeconomic background because I do know that the southern communities are very remote and struggle financially. I would say that this has a huge impact on my community because being a Boston resident makes me very grateful to live in one of the most advanced states for medicine. Potential headline: "North v. South: Does your location impact your access to the coronavirus vaccine?"

I notice that most states in the south have a high level of concern and high levels of each barrier point (a wider area of the illustrated shape). This is in contrast to most northern states, which have relatively low levels of concern and lower lengths of each point, or at least minimal lengths on most points with one outstanding point. 
I wonder if political ideals play into which states have lower or higher levels of concern, as well as which states have more barriers. Is this tied to liberal vs conservative health policies in each state?
Living in Oregon, it looks like our heaviest barriers are low health care resources, historic undervaccination, and irregular medical care. Knowing many people who cannot afford health care or doctors visits, this makes sense to me. I am worried for our community, especially our high houseless population, who are more at risk due to the inability to use healthcare resources. I also know several immunocompromised people who are banking on herd immunity to save them, but when so many people are historically unvaccinated this may not be a safe bet.

comments.raw_comment:
The Next Obstacle For Coronavirus: Vaccine Distribution

After examining this graph we noticed a couple of things such as the Southern states face significantly more barriers to vaccination than the rest of the country, due to lack of or poor health care. Also, Indiana faces the most barriers of all the midwestern states. Another thing we noticed was that Virginia and Colorado have the best health care out of all the states. Smaller states like Massachusetts have easier access to the vaccine and face fewer barriers to rapid vaccination. Lastly, we noticed that several states have good performance in all of the categories except for low health care resources. We have some questions about the graph like why the southern states that lifted their mask mandate have more trouble getting access to the vaccine. We wonder why states in the midwest and east coast have fewer barriers to vaccination unlike the states in the south. We wonder if factors such as population affect certain states from getting more access to the vaccine. This graph impacts our community because it shows how good the state’s health care systems are and if they are able to distribute the vaccine properly, however since we live in Minnesota, according to the graph we have a great health care system and good access to it. This does not mean it is perfect though, which means there are still people struggling to get the vaccine and find good health care.

comments.raw_comment: This graph divides the United States of America into fifty states into bubbles, each bubble has five data points that ultimately represent the risk levels of Covid-19 and any resistance to the use of vaccine within each state. The group noticed a few things about this graph, for one we noticed that the more vaccine-hesitant and higher risk areas were generally clustered in the southern states. In contrast, the east, especially Mssacushets and Connecticut, have the lowest risks of Covid-19 and the most vaccine usage across the country. Our group still remains curious about the accuracy of this graph. We wonder how all this data was collected and about the reliability of the results. We believe that this graph impacts the spread and containment of the coronavirus. Which affects our path back to normality. It appears to affect me and my community because the health care resources are very low in Minnesota and that's where we all live.

comments.raw_comment:
Kaitlin Bryhn, Grace Urban, Evan Divine, and Brian Samuel

The data presented in these graphs led to severing findings that our group noticed. The first thing we found was that the East coast has relatively low concern levels for vaccination barriers. However, New York, Pennsylvania, and Rhode Island share similar concerns for social economic barriers. We also noticed that there are more vaccination barriers in the Southern states. Our own state of Minnesota has a relatively low level of concern. We also wondered why there is such a great divide between the North and the South in vaccination barriers? Could this be a result of certain regions being prioritized for vaccination over other states and what impact does that have on vaccination barriers? Access to vaccinations plays a major role in ensuring that the entire community can be healthy and safe amidst this pandemic. In Minnesota, vaccination access is much better than many other states, although the greatest barrier is low health care resources. Depending on which state you live in, this will affect the role the government plays in mandating policies to curb the spread and distribute vaccinations. Lastly, if your state has a low level of concern, restrictions might be limited and the community might open up sooner. We would title this article, “America’s grasp on vaccines: Vaccination barriers and their fingerprints.”

comments.raw_comment:
While viewing this graph, I noticed how there is a key in the upper right corner that allows the audience to see that purple states depicted on the map have a high concern for coronavirus vaccination barriers while green states have a lower concern. I also noticed how the state of Alaska is surrounded by five factors that may contribute to the high level of concern that this state poses in relation to coronavirus vaccination barriers. It seems that Alaska serves as a key to represent the potential factors that may be restricting vaccination in other states, depending upon which angle the color of the state is shaded in, since each angle points toward a different factor. I wonder why northeastern  states depicted on the map seem to have lower concern than southern and western states. 

The graph illustrates that the state I live in (New York) has a low concern for vaccination barriers. Indeed, I have also seen others in my community, such as teachers and health care professionals, go to get vaccinated rather frequently. This supports the idea that New York has a low concern about vaccination barriers.

The graph depicts the various factors that may contribute to vaccination barriers in each state. As such, a relevant title for this graph may be "What Barriers are Restricting Rapid Vaccination in Your State?" because it is both eye-catching and it reveals the purpose of the graph to the reader without them having to try to understand what information is being presented.

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s radar graphs show the barriers for rapid, widespread vaccination by state and the summarized overall level of concern by state.  If you go to the New York Times article “What Are the Vaccine Roadblocks Where You Live?, you can enter your county and see the barriers for your community.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. We will publish in Friday’s Reveal some of the on-target and catchiest headlines.

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Keep noticing and wondering.  The next graph on world climate risks will be released by Friday, March 26 with moderation on Wednesday, March 31.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice? Level of barrier in states in the South tends to be much higher than other states notably states such as Nev, Okla, Miss, Texas as the color indicate alarming high level of concern. On the other hand, states such in the east coast such as new york and new jersey appear to has little to no barrier that would prevent the coronavirus vaccination. One possible reason for this might due to the fact that states in the east coast are usually richer states with higher incomes families who have less concern when it comes to socioeconomic barriers, health care resources or health care access

What do you wonder? What might be some other possible reason for this to happen?

What impact does this have on you and your community? Currently, I am leaving in the east coast. Seeing how small the barriers of vaccination in my state is really comfort me. This gives a sense of hope that one day, very soon, everyone will get vaccinated
